overview: England between 1000 and 1200 experienced Danish kingship, the Norman Conquest and the rise of the Angevin rulers. Its story also belongs to farmers, craftspeople, scholars, religious communities and families whose work supported royal power. Domesday Book records land and resources, Oxford reveals expanding teaching, and surviving buildings show impressive construction and water management. A London writer even described people skating on polished animal bones. This card covers the map’s two centuries; neither 1000 nor 1200 marks the birth or disappearance of England.

periods.title: English and Danish kings
periods.summary: England was already a kingdom. Cnut’s rule connected it to Denmark and a wider North Sea political world before the succession struggles of 1066.

periods.title: Norman conquest and rebuilding
periods.summary: William’s victory brought new rulers and landholders. Domesday’s survey and the construction of monasteries reveal the reach of the new regime.

periods.title: Angevin rule and growing learning
periods.summary: Henry II and his successors ruled England alongside lands across the Channel. Oxford’s teaching grew while agricultural and religious communities sustained everyday life.

items.text: Cnut ruled England from 1016 to 1035 and Denmark from 1018. For a time, the North Sea linked territories under the same king. England’s history was already connected to neighbors across the water.

William of Normandy defeated Harold at Hastings in October 1066. Conquest changed the ruling elite and control of land, with consequences for the people who worked it. A new king’s victory did not mean a new beginning for every village.

The 1086 Domesday survey asked who held land and what it could produce. Plough teams, mills, fisheries, meadows and woodland mattered to government. It was a remarkable administrative undertaking, but not a census naming every resident.

At Castle Acre, masons built an elaborate priory church over decades. It was consecrated in 1146-1148, and the west end was finished in the 1160s. The stonework is evidence of skilled labor, planning and patrons able to command substantial resources.

A plough team in the Domesday teaching sources consisted of eight oxen. Farming demanded animals, equipment and coordinated labor. Picture steering that team before imagining a medieval farmer working alone with a little garden shovel.

Domesday distinguishes freemen, villagers, smallholders and enslaved people. These categories reveal unequal rights and obligations. A landowner’s household and a family bound to agricultural service did not experience the kingdom in the same way.

Queen Edith sponsored a book about her husband, Edward the Confessor. Family ties, property and patronage gave some elite women political influence. Queens are much easier to find in written records than most working women, so their lives cannot stand for everyone’s.

In 1173 William FitzStephen described Londoners skating on frozen Moorfields marshes. They tied polished animal bones to their feet and pushed with iron-tipped poles. Winter sport, medieval equipment: the wheels were definitely optional.

Teaching existed at Oxford by 1096, but the university has no known exact founding date. It grew rapidly after 1167, and by about 1190 a student from Friesland appears in its story. Learning crossed borders as well as generations.

The Bayeux embroidery tells the story of the conquest through pictures and Latin captions. One reads “ISTI PORTANT ARMAS AD NAVES”: “These men carry arms to the ships.” The cited catalogue preserves this wording in an 1821 copy of the medieval work. Latin here is a written narrative language, not a claim about what every family spoke at home.

Castle Acre’s monks had an infirmary and used herbs within a medical tradition concerned with balancing bodily humors. The herb garden displayed there today is a reconstruction. Such evidence tells us about monastic care, not equal access to treatment across England.

Castle Acre’s communal latrine was built over a water channel, with an upper level accessible from the dormitory. Its design carried waste away using flowing water. Even a monastery devoted to spiritual life needed to solve the very earthly problem of where the poo went.

ending.text: England did not fall in 1200. John had become king in 1199, and the kingdom continued through later political and religious changes. The endpoint here belongs to the imported map coverage, while learning, settlement and household life continued beyond it.
